title: Recycling and the Great Pacific Garbage Patch
summary: Josh and Chuck return from holiday break and discuss recycling, starting with the 1970s anti-littering campaign and the Crying Indian ad. They cover the history of curbside newspaper recycling (first program 1973 in University City, Missouri) and the shift to single stream recycling, with its magnets, lasers, and air puffs sorting materials. They debate whether recycling is worthwhile, citing an economist's claim that it can be more harmful than good, and discuss tipping fees at landfills, the commodity value of recyclables, and the 2008 price drop for recycled mixed paper. They explain how to recycle at home (rinse containers, separate labels and caps), and warn against PVC (resin code 3) because it is hard to recycle and contains phthalates. The main topic is plastic pollution: UN figures on plastic in the ocean, plastic that breaks into 'mermaid's tears' (nurdles), and the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre, the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, which is roughly twice the size of Texas. About 80 percent of ocean trash starts on land. The episode ends with listener mail: corrections about the body armor episode (Sergeant Donald Anderson, Apache helicopter engine), spider silk produced in goats' milk, and a name correction for listener Coss Bates Stahl.

segments.title: Opening banter and holiday return
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck return from holiday break, joke about the studio, and reminisce about 1970s and 1990s recycling and littering campaigns.

segments.title: Curbside recycling and single stream sorting
segments.summary: The first curbside newspaper recycling program started in 1973 in University City, Missouri, and took off in the 1990s. Single stream recycling, which puts everything in one bin, uses magnets, infrared lasers, and air puffs to sort materials with little human contact.

segments.title: Is recycling worth it? Tipping fees and commodity value
segments.summary: The hosts discuss skeptics who think recycling does nothing, and an economist's claim that recycling can be more harmful than good. They explain landfill tipping fees (about 42 dollars a ton on average in 2008) and why recyclables are commodities that sell for money, with recycled mixed paper once fetching about 90 dollars a ton before the price dropped.

segments.title: Home recycling tips and PVC plastic
segments.summary: Tips for home recycling: clean containers and separate labels and caps from bottles. Plastic with a number 3 (PVC) should be avoided because it is hard to recycle and contains phthalates, which are harmful.

segments.title: Plastic in the ocean and the Great Pacific Garbage Patch
segments.summary: A UN study found about 46,000 pieces of floating plastic per square mile of ocean in 2006. Plastic breaks into small pieces (mermaid's tears, nurdles) that filter feeders eat and that absorb toxins. The North Pacific Subtropical Gyre, the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, is about twice the size of Texas and connected to a second gyre by a long trash trail. About 80 percent of ocean trash starts on land.

segments.title: Ways to help reduce ocean plastic
segments.summary: Because most ocean trash starts on land, individuals can help by avoiding plastic grocery bags and recycling everything they can. The hosts note related articles on the site.

segments.title: Listener mail and corrections
segments.summary: Corrections about the body armor episode, including Sergeant Donald Anderson, who works on the T700 turbine engine of the Apache helicopter. Listeners explained that spider silk is produced in goats' milk. A name correction is made for listener Coss Bates Stahl.
